content: The Roundabout (Robo) family of proteins consists of single-pass transmembrane receptors that are highly conserved across various animal species, ranging from C. elegans to humans. These proteins were initially discovered in Drosophila through mutant screens aimed at identifying genes involved in axon guidance. The name roundabout was derived from the mutant phenotype observed in Drosophila, which resembled circular traffic junctions. Robo receptors are most recognized for their critical role in nervous system development, where they respond to secreted Slit ligands. A well-studied example of this interaction is the Slit-Robo signaling pathway, which is essential for regulating axonal midline crossing. This signaling pathway also plays a pivotal role in other neurodevelopmental processes, such as the formation of the olfactory tract, optic nerve, and motor axon fasciculation. Beyond the nervous system, Slit-Robo signaling contributes to cell migration and the development of various tissues, including the lung, kidney, liver, muscle, and breast. Mutations in Robo genes have been implicated in several neurodevelopmental disorders in humans. A large-scale genetic screen in Drosophila identified the roundabout (robo) mutation, which caused axons to improperly cross and recross the midline. Subsequent research revealed that the secreted protein Slit serves as the ligand for the Robo receptor. Vertebrate Slit proteins were later identified and shown to bind both vertebrate and Drosophila Robo receptors, mediating axonal repulsion in spinal cord explants. Functional analyses of vertebrate Slit and Robo mutants demonstrated that Slit-Robo signaling also regulates commissural axon guidance in vertebrates. While vertebrate Robo1 and Robo2 mediate repulsion in response to Slit to prevent inappropriate midline crossing, Robo3/Rig1 was found to have a unique function: it promotes midline crossing, unlike the other Robo receptors. Phylogenetic studies indicate that all Robo receptors evolved from a common ancestral protein, with subsequent diversification occurring independently in different lineages. The Robo gene was first identified in Drosophila and has since been cloned in various species, including mice and humans. Drosophila possesses three Robo receptors (Robo1, Robo2, and Robo3), while vertebrates have four (Robo1, Robo2, Robo3/Rig1, and Robo4/Magic Roundabout). In mice, Robo1 and Robo2 genes are located on chromosome 16, while Robo3 and Robo4 are found on chromosome 9. In vertebrates, Robo1 undergoes complex alternative splicing, producing several isoforms, including DUTT1, which has been identified as a tumor suppressor gene. Similarly, Robo3/Rig1 is alternatively spliced, generating two splice products that are expressed at different times during commissural axon guidance and exhibit opposing activities. In humans, Robo1 is broadly expressed throughout the central nervous system. Robo2 is enriched in most regions of the adult and fetal brain, as well as in the adult ovary, with intermediate expression in the fetal liver and adult lung, kidney, spleen, testes, and spinal cord. Robo3/Rig1 is found in the hindbrain and spinal cord, while Robo4 is expressed in the heart, liver, lungs, kidneys, muscle, small intestine, endothelial cells, and predominantly in the placenta. Structurally, Robo proteins share a conserved architecture, including five immunoglobulin-like domains, three fibronectin type III (FN3) repeats, a transmembrane domain, and a cytoplasmic domain with up to four conserved motifs (CC0-3). In all Robo receptors except vertebrate Robo4, the Ig1 and Ig2 domains are evolutionarily conserved and are critical for binding Slit ligands. Robo4 is unique in that it contains only two Ig and FN3 domains, although recent research suggests that vertebrate Slit2 can bind to Robo4. Robo proteins are essential regulators of axonal midline crossing during nervous system development in bilaterian animals, including insects and mammals. In Drosophila embryos, Robo1 and Robo2 prevent ipsilaterally projecting axons from crossing the midline and ensure that contralateral axons do not remain stuck at the midline. Robo3, while also binding Slit, does not play a major role in midline crossing regulation but is required for lateral pathway selection of axons after crossing. Robo2 also contributes to lateral pathway formation. In the vertebrate spinal cord, Robo1 and Robo2 are expressed on commissural axons and act as repulsive receptors for Slit ligands secreted by floor plate cells at the midline. In contrast, Robo3/Rig1 is required for midline crossing and functions, in part, by antagonizing Slit-mediated repulsion via Robo1 and Robo2. Robo receptors also regulate other axon pathfinding decisions during development, such as axonal projections in the optic tract and olfactory epithelium. The Robo gene family also guides and regulates the migration of non-neuronal cells, including neuronal precursor cells, muscle cells, tracheal cells, Langerhans cells, and vascular smooth muscle cells. Robo1 is thought to inhibit glioma invasion and migration. Glioblastoma cells tend to grow away from areas with high concentrations of Slit2 and its receptor Robo1, suggesting that the Robo1/Slit2 complex acts as a chemorepellent, inhibiting tumor cell invasion and migration. The binding of Slit to Robo receptors leads to reorganization of the actin cytoskeleton. Actin polymerization is regulated by several adaptor proteins that bind to the cytoplasmic motifs of Robo receptors. In Drosophila, downstream signaling proteins of Robo1 include Enabled, Son of Sevenless (SOS), Rac, and Dock. Activation of Robo1 by Slit increases actin depolymerization, resulting in growth cone collapse. The signaling mechanisms of Drosophila Robo2 and Robo3 remain unclear, although studies suggest they have distinct signaling capabilities that cannot be replicated by Robo1. The vertebrate Robo3/Rig1 homolog is a more distant relative of the Robo gene family and plays a distinct role in axonal guidance. Robo3/Rig1 is alternatively spliced to produce a protein that inhibits Robo1/2-mediated repulsion, thereby promoting midline crossing. The exact mechanism by which Robo3 achieves this anti-repulsive activity remains unknown. Robo4 has been linked to angiogenesis in mice and zebrafish and is present in human microvascular endothelial cells (HMVEC) and human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVEC). Exposure of Robo4 to Slit2 inhibits angiogenesis, but exposure to a protein that inhibits Slit2 also inhibits angiogenesis. These conflicting results suggest that the role of Robo4 in blood vessel growth is not fully understood. Robo1 has been associated with both tumor growth and suppression. The Slit2/Robo1 pathway has been implicated in tumor angiogenesis, leading to subsequent tumor growth. Slit2 proteins have been identified in various tumors, including melanoma, breast cancer, small cell lung cancer, and bladder cancer. Inhibition of the Slit2/Robo1 pathway via R5 and RoboN reduced tumor mass and volume while also decreasing microvessel density. However, Slit2 proteins have not been identified in all tumor types, and other research suggests that Slit2 expression may suppress tumors in small cell lung cancer and breast cancer. Robo1 has been associated with dyslexia, potentially through chromosomal translocation, although its role in this condition is not fully understood. A genome-wide linkage study suggested that the Robo2 gene may be involved in developmental disorders such as psychopathy. A defect in the Robo3/Rig1 protein results in horizontal gaze palsy with progressive scoliosis (HGPPS), a rare genetic disorder. HGPPS is characterized by the absence of horizontal eye movement within the socket (while vertical movement remains unaffected) and the gradual curvature of the spine during development. This disorder is caused by a genetic mutation on chromosome 11 and is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. During normal brain development, Robo3/Rig1 reduces the sensitivity of Robo1 to Slit proteins, allowing axons to grow past the midline. This process enables axons to cross to the opposite side of the brain, which is crucial for motor function and sensory processing. In HGPPS patients, the absence of Robo3/Rig1 prevents axons in the corticospinal tract and trochlear nerve from growing past the midline. This abnormal growth in the hindbrain and spinal cord manifests as the symptoms associated with HGPPS.
